The folders inside a backup are chosen in a tree instead of guessed, any container, VM or folder set can point at a repository you wrote down once, and you can sign in with a passkey.

## ✨ Added

- **Choose the folders a container backup covers, in a tree.** A container backup used to be all of its appdata or nothing, with a list of exclude patterns typed by hand as the only way to trim it. Every mount the container has is now a root you can expand, and you tick what the backup covers. Ticking a parent takes everything under it, unticking one subfolder leaves that branch out, and a half-filled box says the branch is partly covered without you having to open it.

  Three things make that trustworthy rather than merely clickable. Each root carries a **live count** of the paths the next backup will hand restic, so narrowing something shows a number that moves. Each root carries a **collapsible list of its own exclusions**, so what you left out is reviewable later rather than remembered. And a selection that covers less than the last saved one says so, in the editor, naming what changes: from the next backup on, snapshots contain only the selected folders, and existing snapshots are untouched.

  A container you never touch keeps automatic detection exactly as before. **Reset selection** puts a container that has been narrowed back to it, and the confirmation names every consequence including the cache-folder settings, because it clears those too.
- **The same tree on the Folders page.** A folder set is one folder, and everything under it came along. **Choose folders** on the set's row opens the same control over the set's own path, with the same count and the same exclusions list. Unticking the last folder is refused rather than saved, because a set that covers nothing is a set that should be deleted, and the refusal says so.

  Changing a set's folder clears its selection, and the dialog says that before you change it, not afterwards. A restore is mapped onto the paths the chosen snapshot actually holds, so restoring an older snapshot of a narrowed set restores what is in it rather than failing on a path that was excluded after it was taken. An in-place restore where none of the selectors map to anything in the snapshot is aborted with the reason instead of quietly restoring everything.
- **Skip cache folders, per root** (`CACHEDIR.TAG`). Browser caches, thumbnail caches and build caches mark themselves with a tag file that restic can be told to obey. The switch sits under the root it belongs to, and it says plainly that it applies to the whole backup of that container rather than to that one folder, because that is what the flag does.
- **Named repositories** ([#204](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/bombvault/issues/204)). "I would like to back up a VM or folder directly to a B2 or NAS share, bypassing the primary backup location." Half of that already worked: a domain's Backup Path takes a restic remote, so Folders as a whole could go straight to B2. What it could not do was move **one** item.

  Write the locations down once in **Settings > Storage > Repositories**, then pick one on a container, a VM or a folder set. A row shows its name, its location, whether it is reachable and how many items point at it, so the interface can refuse something before the attempt rather than only in the error afterwards. Two refusals, both from the same fact - nothing ever re-homes a backup that has been written: the location of a repository in use cannot be moved, and a repository in use cannot be deleted.

  Changing an item's repository is likewise refused once it has backups. A rename strands snapshots loudly; a moved repository strands them silently, because the next backup into the new location succeeds and nothing ever reports an error. Every item that is left alone follows its domain's repository exactly as before, and the picker spells that out ("the domain repository") rather than offering a blank line. A whole-domain prune or integrity check still works on the domain repository and says so; retention follows the item.
- **Passkeys.** Sign in with the key on a phone, a laptop or a security stick, alongside the password and never instead of it.

  The constraint is part of the feature. WebAuthn binds a credential to a domain name, and browsers refuse the exchange on a bare IP address and again on a certificate they do not trust. The Unraid template opens `https://[IP]:3443` with a certificate covering only localhost, so the **default installation is exactly the case that cannot work**. Rather than let the browser answer with an unexplained error, the server refuses with a sentence naming the reason, the card prints it before anybody clicks, and the login screen hides the button instead of offering one that fails. Behind a proxy with a real name and a trusted certificate it works.

  A key is stored with the address it belongs to, and the list marks the ones that cannot answer here rather than hiding them, so a key you registered elsewhere does not look lost. The password always remains: removing every passkey locks nobody out, because a lost phone must not mean losing the tool that recovers everything else.

## 🎨 Design

- **The Recovery tab wears the house heading like every other tab.** It was a size smaller and a shade dimmer than the twelve pages around it, so the tab with the most frightening job in the app - the one somebody opens after losing their configuration - had the quietest heading in it. A source scan over every page keeps them together; Glyphs and Login are named exceptions.
- **The login screen shows the mark.** It is the one surface with no rail, which left it an unlabelled password box on a plain background.
- **The page column reaches the rail.** It stopped 24 pixels short of it, from the wrapper's own bottom padding sitting inside the scroll container, so it could never be scrolled away. The other three sides keep their gutter.
- **The save mark is the shared one**, the same drawing from the same file every app of mine uses.
- **Three ways to give, in one row**, on the About card and in the README, saying the same thing in every language.
- **The two notes under a passkey get a separator.** Whether the second note is there at all depends on the authenticator, so the separator belongs in the markup rather than as a full stop on the first sentence that would dangle without it.

## ⚡ Improved

- **Every line in the activity log says which domain it belongs to** ([#200](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/bombvault/issues/200)). A line carried the item's name and nothing else, and a container and a folder set can easily share one. Somebody chasing a running backup read "Backing up HomeDVR", went to the Folders tab, and found the set of that name sitting idle, because it was the container of that name that was running. The domain was in the data the whole time, since it drives the filter above the log; it just never reached the line.
- **A failure about a repository says which repository** ([#206](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/bombvault/issues/206)). "Fatal: create repository at s3:http:[path]:8333[path] failed" - the path scrubber had eaten the address, because its pattern matches any run of slash-led tokens and a repository URL looks exactly like one. A remote location is the operator's own storage layout, not a credential, so those are left whole now while everything around them is still scrubbed. A local repository stays scrubbed: it is a path on this box, indistinguishable from the appdata and mount paths the scrubber exists for. The exemption brings its own credential scrubber anchored to the location's structure, so a password containing a slash cannot ride out inside one.
- **Setting a password no longer locks you out in the same breath.** The route that turns the login on is reachable without a session only while the login is off, so the request that enabled it was the last one that browser was allowed to make: every control answered 401 until the page was reloaded and the password typed again. Setting up the second factor is what somebody does next, so that was the visible casualty. The response now carries the session it just made necessary, and clearing the password sends the cookie away.
- **Go 1.27, and the whole dependency front brought current** - React 19.3, Vite 8.3, Vitest 5, ESLint 10.10, TypeScript-ESLint 8.70, React Router 7.18, and the base images with them.

## 🐛 Fixed

- **The Stop button was on one page out of five** ([#200](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/bombvault/issues/200)). v8.7.0 said a running backup shows a progress bar with a Stop button beside it. That was true of folder sets and of nothing else: containers, VMs, flash and config showed the bar and offered no way to act on it, while the server had been registering a cancel for all five and the endpoint had been accepting every one of those keys the whole time. The button is on every card that can run a backup now, with the same two conditions the Folders page used: only while the run is active, and never during a restore, which keeps its own control and its own warning about a half-restored target.

## 🌐 Translations

- The Repositories card, the per-item picker and both of its refusals in all 42 languages.
- The folder-selection tree in all 42: the disclosure, the live count, the exclusions list, the cache-folder switch and its scope line, the narrowing note and the reset confirmation.
- The passkey card, its explanation of why an IP address cannot work, and the per-key address notes in all 42.
- The activity log's domain labels, taken from the names the tabs already carry in each language rather than translated afresh.
